summary:
Alabama stands under the United States national framework, which applies in every state. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, defines sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, bars transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibits self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.

Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on what documentation to consider and how name and gender changes interact with federal records.

Entry screening carries its own exposure. In February 2025 the State Department announced a ban on trans athletes entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent ban on grounds of fraud. At United States checkpoints, TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy and can out a traveller. In April 2025 several foreign governments issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules, and in March 2025 at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country.

Within Alabama, access to facilities according to gender identity is prohibited. The state enacted facility bans in 2022 and 2024, and the July 2026 Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment records that Alabama's "Don't Say Gay" bill carries a bathroom ban extending to college campuses, placing the state in the assessment's worst-law grouping of legislatively-eroding jurisdictions. Visitors using restrooms, changing facilities or campus facilities inconsistent with sex assigned at birth fall within these prohibitions.

Violence against trans women is documented at a rate of 3.8 per 100,000 per year in Alabama, calculated on a 428-victim national base for 2008 to 2025 and treated by its authors as an undercount floor rather than a full count. Alabama is graded in the worst-law group on the same national analysis.
tangentialFactors:
Facility prohibitions are a national pattern rather than an Alabama peculiarity. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states, while 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban and some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances.

Enforcement of such bans has produced arrests. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law.

Document rules are tightening elsewhere in the country. In February 2026 Kansas enacted a law preventing transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences, invalidating existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups describe it as a template for other states, with further bills pending. A July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the latest "Do Not Travel" state for trans people, bringing the total to four states so flagged, and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights while federal policies drove nationwide trends.

Detention and custody carry documented harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs; the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In ICE custody, transgender men have reportedly faced forced-labour programmes with refusals met by beatings, solitary confinement and reports of severe sexual abuse. In December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting "radical gender ideology" and characterised as "domestic terrorist groups", and a May 2026 White House counterterrorism strategy stated that activities would prioritise groups whose ideology is "anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist". Advocates have compared these actions to the early stages of genocide.

Care access is constrained nationally for visitors who need it. Executive Order 14187 (January 2025) described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," leading some hospitals to pause care, and in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18, and gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.
localsOnly:
Alabama residents are themselves barred from using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity under laws enacted in 2022 and 2024, with the extension of the ban to college campuses recorded in the July 2026 risk assessment. The same assessment groups Alabama among legislatively-erasing jurisdictions with the worst laws for trans people.

Residents share the federal documentation regime: Alabama birth certificates and licences are state-issued, while passports and visas follow the national rules, so a resident holding an X-marker passport may renew only into an M or F marker after the existing document expires.

Community violence is a resident-facing condition as well as a visitor risk. The 3.8 per 100,000 annual killing rate for trans women is derived from national tracking of 428 victims between 2008 and 2025 and is presented as a floor, meaning the lived figure for residents is at least that high.
outOfScopeNotes:
The penalties attached to Alabama's 2022 and 2024 facility bans, including whether violation is a criminal offence, are not sourced in the current inventory; only the existence and dates of the bans and their extension to college campuses are documented here.

Whether Alabama restricts changes to gender markers on state birth certificates or driver's licences is unresolved. The inventory documents Kansas's February 2026 statute but does not state Alabama's own document rules.

The enactment status and current litigation posture of the Alabama "Don't Say Gay" bill described in the July 2026 assessment are not stated in the source; the claim reproduced here is that the bill carries a bathroom ban extending to college campuses and that Alabama sits in the assessment's worst-law grouping.

The 3.8 per 100,000 figure rests on a national victim base of 428 killings between 2008 and 2025 compiled by outside researchers; its authors describe it as an undercount floor, and the inventory does not document the underlying counting methodology, the population denominator used, or whether any of those killings occurred in Alabama rather than being attributed to it.

Whether Alabama state law restricts gender-affirming care for minors, and whether the state participates in or resists the federal care measures described in the national framework, is not sourced here.
